entry.title: A New Build System For This Website

content.p: My website started with just HTML I wrote, with a bit of CSS. But I don't really like HTML, and I do like really GNU Emacs, so I started using Org Mode, exporting each bit manually. But I don't really like doing the same thing over and over and over again, so I wrote a bash script to handle it for me.

code.span:
echo "Blog

Blog Entries

Back Home
    " > blog.html

content.p: It's not the most elegant thing in the word, but it does the trick. Besides, bash is just about never elegant anyway, that's what I like about it – like a more cursed perl.
Maybe now that I just run a script to setup my website, I might even start actually putting something on this blog! Might even make an RSS feed too, but not yet…
I also might end up automating the part where I push to Github, but not yet.

entry.title: Minecraft Modding on 1.8.9: First Fun With Forge

content.p: Go over to where your Forge zip was unziped, and open src/main/java/com/example/examplemod/ExampleMod.java. Now, change MODID to whatever you want your mod to be called

code.span: public static final String MODID = "Cam's Mod";

content.p: And then set the version number to "0.1".

And from the root of your project (the same folder as gradlew.bat), and run .\gradlew.bat runClient. If you've done everything right, then this'll (after a bit of loading) start Minecraft 1.8.9 with forge, and if you look at the mods section, you should see yours! And if you now click on it, you'll see that there's no description; lets change that.
Go to src/main/resources/mcmod.info, and change it to this.

span.span: // Note that this has to match whatever you set MODID to in the Java file.
// Note that this has to match whatever you set VERSION to in the Java file.
// I haven't made this yet, so don't bother trying.
"This wouldn't have been possible without the Forge documentation, minecraftforum.net, and whoever discovered caffeine."

content.p: And now launch the game again, and it should show up with that description when you select it in the mod menu! This is in a format called JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), which is common among the programming industry (along with its competitors, XML, and Sexps).

We discussed Gradle a bit in the last entry, but we didn't go into too much detail. As mentioned last time, Gradle automates compiling all of the code, and it's not just used in Minecraft, but all across the programming industry.
As it turns out, there exists other Gradle commands we can run as well (who'd of thought…)

ul.li: \.gradlew test will run all of the unit tests (this will be discussed further in a later entry).
\.gradlew runServer will start a modded Minecraft server.
\.gradlew help will tell you all of the other commands available.

content.p: Now you might be wondering why the command is gradlew, when the program is called Gradle. This is because Gradle creates a wrapper script (a script to run itself), that makes sure all of the necessary programs are installed to the correct version, and that Gradle is being used properly. You can of course, just use Gradle directly (say, running gradle runClient), but this isn't recommended, and might not work as expected due to versioning issues.

Now, run the classic javac Animal.java Chicken.java Main.java, and then java Main.
Recall Main.java and Student.java from a previous post. Try making a general Person.java, that both Student.java and Employee.java inherit from.

I need to do a group project in Javafor uni, and as a team, we decided on using Maven. However, not everyone on the team knows how to use Maven, so I've written this up – I hope that it can be useful for you.

Apache Maven is a build system for (among other languages) Java. It describes how the system should be built using XML (eXtensible Markup Language), as well as any dependencies the project needs, and any plugins Maven should be using. This all goes into a file called pom.xml, in the root of your project's directory.
Suppose we have some project – we may lay out the build file like this.
Pretty scary right. This is the pom.xml file for a project I'm doing at university for a module.

Notice how we're not specifying where to find the source code, like we would in say, Apache Ant, GNU Makefiles, or a hacked-together perl scsript. Maven goes for convention over configuration, and defaults to the following structures:

tr.td: The root of the project, and where pom.xml lives
Contains the tests (Junit tests, in our case)

content.p: We can then compile our program using the mvn compile command. This will – if it doesn't already exist – create target/, a directory in which all class files go, as well as any jars that may be generated.
Maven has many built in commands, and we can add more by using plugins. Some of the basic and most useful commands are as follows:

ul.li: mvn compile Compiles the source into class files
mvn package Compiles the source into a jar file
mvn install Install the package in the local Maven repository
mvn clean Remove build files from target/

content.p: If you're using IntelliJ, congratulations, you don't really need to use these commands, as it'll be handled by IntelliJ. However, if you're using another editor (say, GNU Emacs), then you may need to do this yourself (if you're a fellow Emacs lover, then I'd recommend just using M-x compile, and running Maven commands through that – I might write a transient menu for it at some point). We can also add some more commands, using the amazing magic of ✨ plugins ✨.
I have some projects I have to do for uni, some of which require JavaFX (ew). To do this, we use a plugin.
We can now run mvn javafx:run, and our JavaFX plugin will be started! (Okay, technically we also need to include JavaFX as a dependency, but I'm covering that in the next section, not here).

Suppose I have some project, for which I want to use Junit 5, and Maven. But oh no! I can't run that directly through Maven, whatever shall I do :'( ! Thankfully, dependencies come to the rescue; for our Junit example, we could include something like this
We can now run mvn test, and all tests within src/test/java/ will be ran.
If we also want to include, say, JavaFX, we can add that as a dependency too!
Now, when we run mvn javafx:run, the program will be started.

entry.title: Minecraft Modding on 1.8.9: Setting up Java

content.p: So you want to program a Minecraft mod for 1.8.9. It's a niche genre of person who wants to do that, I can respect it. If you only came here for source code examples, they can be found on my Github here.

The first thing you're going to need is a JDK, or Java Development Toolkit, and for 1.8.9, you'll need Java 8 specifically. I personally use OpenJDK, which can be downloaded here, and you'll want the version starting with OpenJDK8U-jdk_<your-cpu-arch>_<your-OS>. For example, if you're on windows, with a 64 bit x64 CPU, then you download OpenJDK8U-jdk_x64_windows_hotspot_8u482b08.msi (if you don't know which is you, it's probably this one). After getting that, you'll also need the 1.8.9 MDK (Minecraft Development Toolkit), git, and GNU Emacs
And if you don't already have a Github account, now would probably be the time to make one (much like the editor, it doesn't have to be Github, but I'll be focusing on it).

After going through the Java installer, go into powershell, and go to wherever you downloaded the MDK zip to. You can either do this by opening the folder in File Explorer, right clicking, and clicking open in terminal, or by using the cd command, which would look something like this (cd stands for "change directory"; directory is just another name for folder).
Then, create a new directory called minecraft-forge-1.8.9, move the MDK zip file into it, and then unzip it. Again, you can do this with the File Explorer, or with a command.

Now, simply run .\gradlew.bat runClient, and modded Minecraft will start (note that it might take a while trying to download things). Granted, there are barely any running in it, but we'll fix that soon enough.

gradlew.bat is a little program that controls something called Gradle. Gradle is a build system, which is a piece of software that helps us compile and run code. Some projects have thousands of files, and it would be a pain to compile each of those by hand, so these programs do it for us.

First, download Emacs from https://www.gnu.org/software/emacs/. Then, download https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vibe-876/java-tutorial-code/refs/heads/main/init.el, and place it at ~/.emacs.d/init.el. This will be the text editor we'll use – it should be fairly straight forward to figure out what that script is doing, but if not, it'll be explained as we go.
Create a new folder, and put two Java files into it – Main.java, and Student.java, and then write the following into them. For Student.java, write

code.span: * A basic call for describing a student at a school.
* @param firstName the first name of the student
* @param lastName the last name of the student
* @param age the age of the student
public Student(String firstName, String lastName, int age) {
* Getter function for the students name. Combines the firstName
* @return the full name of the student
* Getter function for the students age, int years.
* Increases the students age in years.
* @param howManyYearsOlder how many years older the student now is
* Checks if the student is 18 yet.
* @return true if the student is older than 18, and false otherwise

content.p: And for Main.java, write

code.span: * Adds a new student. Warning: will crash if less than three arguments
* @param args the students first name, followed by their last name, followed by their age
System.out.println("Student " + newStudent.getName() + " is " + newStudent.getAge() + " years old.");

content.p: Now, you can run javac Main.java Student.java, and then java Main Gerard Way 49 (yes I was listening to MCR while writing this, how could you tell?) in the terminal (after opening this as a project, of course). What happens if you don't include any arguments to Main?

ol.li: Make it so the program doesn't crash when you don't give it good arguments. This is sometimes known as defensive programming.
Add your own JavaDoc (the special comments) for the things you've edited, and give yourself credit with an @author tag.
Add a new feature to Student.java, that changes the student's name. After this, try changing Main.java so that the fourth argument is the new name of the student.
